chunk.chapter_title: 36. Ravana reveals his Project to him
chunk.text:
Passing over to the further side of that Lord of the Waters, 
the Ocean, Ravana saw a solitary hermitage, an ancient and 
holy retreat in the middle of a forest. 
There he found the 
Demon Maricha clad in a black antelope skin, wearing matted 
locks and given up to the practice of asceticism. 
Ravana having approached him, Maricha, according to 
tradition, entertained him in many ways not known to man. 
Placing pure food and water before his sovereign, he humbly 
addressed him saying :-
" Is all well with Lanka, 0 Chief of the Titans ? With what 
purpose hast thou come hither again so speedily ? " 
· 
On hearing this enquiry, the mighty and eloquent Ravana 
answered in this wise :-
CHAPTER 36 
Rtwana refJeals his Project to the Demon Maricha 
" 0 MAluCHA, listen to me as I relate everything to thee I 0 
My Child, I am deeply aiHicted and thou alone canst temper 
my distress I 
" Thou art conversant with J anasthana, it was there that my 
brother Khara, the long-armed Dushana, my sister Shur-
panakha and the powerful Trishiras and other flesh-eating 
titans, prowlers of the night, had at my command taken up 
their residence, in order to harass the sages in that vast forest, 
who were engaged in their austerities. 
" Fourteen thousand titans of terrible deeds, full of courage 
and supremely skilled, dwelt in Janasthana under the leadership 
of Khara. 
These powerful warriors assembled there, met 
with Rams in the field. 
Furnished with every kind of weapon, 
clad in mail, and headed by Khara, they were assailed by the 
iofuriated Rams, without a single provocative word having 
been uttered, who directed the arrows of his bow against 
them, and under the fiery darts of a mere mortal, fighting 
single-handed and on foot, those fourteen thousand titans of 
grest prowess fell ; Khara perished in that struggle and Dushana 
76

ARANYA KANDA 
was laid low with Trisbiras also ; peace was thus established in 
the Dandaka Forest. 
" Having been exiled to the forest with his wife by an out-
raged sire, that insignificant mortal, Rama, the obloquy of the 
warrior class, a man without moral 
principle, ruthless, 
passionate, fanatical, acquisitive and a slave to his senses, 
dwells in his hermitage, having forsworn his duty. Essentially 
unjust, seeking to harm others without cause, depending on 
his own strength alone, he has mutilated my sister by cutting 
off her ears and nose. 
" I have resolved to carry off his consort, Sita, by force, who 
resembles a daughter of the Gods, and I now solicit thine aid 
in this undertaking. 
0 Hero, I with my brothers have nothing 
to fear from the Gods, therefore do thou accompany me as 
a loyal ally; 0 Titan; thou hast no equal in pride and courage 
in battle and in strategy; thou art also a master, being versed 
in the laws of magic. 
" Learn from me how thou canst best assist me ! Assuming 
the form of a golden deer, flecked with silver, do thou pass to 
and fro near Rama's hermitage in the presence of Sita. Seeing 
that lovely doe, assuredly Sita will say to her lord and 
Lakshmana :-c Do ye capture it!' 
" When they are far distant and, by good fortune, Sita is 
left alone, I shall bear her away without hindrance, as Rahu 
devours the splendour of the moon. The abduction of his 
consort will cause Rama to die of grief, and I shall regain my 
happiness and security in a heart wholly satisfied ! " 
Hearing these words concerning Sita, the benevolent features 
of Maricha wilted with terror and, passing his tongue over 
his dry lips, with a fixed gaze like unto one dead, he regarded 
Ravana. Filled with dread, knowing well the defence of the 
forest to be valiantly upheld by Rama, with joined palms 
Maricha addressed Ravana in words tending to his welfare :-

brief.summary_1line: Ravana visits the ascetic demon Maricha and reveals his plan to abduct Sita by using Maricha disguised as a golden deer to lure Rama away.

image_candidates.scene_text: Ravana stands before the ascetic Maricha in a lonely forest hermitage, outlining his scheme while the demon listens in growing terror.
Ravana describes the magical plan of a golden deer flecked with silver wandering before Rama’s forest hut to entice Sita.
Maricha, pale and trembling with dry lips and folded hands, stares at Ravana in dread upon hearing Sita’s name and the plan.

deep.rich_summary: Ravana crosses the ocean and visits the forest hermitage of the demon Maricha, who has withdrawn into an ascetic life. After being received with ritual hospitality, Ravana explains the disaster at Janasthana: Rama single‑handedly slew Khara, Dushana, Trishiras, and fourteen thousand titans, avenging the mutilation of Ravana’s sister Shurpanakha. Burning with anger and humiliation, Ravana unveils a calculated plan for revenge. He intends to abduct Rama’s wife, Sita, believing her loss will destroy Rama with grief. To accomplish this, he asks Maricha—skilled in illusion—to transform into a dazzling golden deer that will lure Rama and Lakshmana away from the hermitage. The scheme marks the fateful beginning of the plot that will lead to Sita’s abduction and the great war to come.

highlight_spans.why: Ravana’s arrival at the lonely forest hermitage introduces the meeting that will set the central deception of the epic in motion.
Ravana recounts the staggering defeat of fourteen thousand demons by Rama alone, underscoring Rama’s mythic power.
Ravana’s fury over Shurpanakha’s mutilation and his contemptuous description of Rama reveal the emotional motive behind his revenge.
The crucial revelation: Ravana declares his plan to abduct Sita and asks Maricha to help execute it.
The magical strategy is explained—Maricha must transform into a golden deer to lure Rama away from Sita.

top_scenes.scene_text: Ravana, towering and regal, arrives at the lonely forest hermitage where the ascetic demon Maricha sits in black antelope skin beneath ancient trees.
Ravana passionately describing Rama’s slaughter of fourteen thousand demons while Maricha listens in tense silence inside the shadowed hermitage.
Ravana outlining the plot as an illusory golden deer gleams in imagination before them—its silver‑flecked hide glowing like magic in the forest dusk.
